processing: Little is documented for this tea; as with other Dian Hong gongfu, the leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried. The name suggests fine, thread-like leaf.
harvest_season: Not documented for this name. Bud-heavy Dian Hong is generally picked in early spring.
appearance_dry: Little is documented; the name, golden silk, suggests fine golden threads.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear orange-red, as with other tippy Dian Hong.
appearance_wet: Typically soft coppery buds and young leaf, as with other tippy Dian Hong.
taste_profile: Little is documented for this tea. Expect the honeyed, malty sweetness typical of bud-rich Dian Hong.

brewing.notes: General advice for tippy Dian Hong: buds extract quickly, so keep the water a little off the boil and the early steeps short.

vintage_note: No selling convention is recorded for this name. Like other Dian Hong it is usually sold by the current year's harvest, with early spring tippy lots costing more, and is best drunk within a couple of years.
description:
Jin Si, golden silk, is a Dian Hong name that describes looks: fine golden threads. It appears in sellers' lists alongside other grade names, including Jin Ya, the golden-bud grade, but no standard defining it turned up, so treat it as a trade name.

How it is made is not documented in any detail. Assume normal gongfu black tea work on Yunnan leaf, and do not assume it is pure bud unless the seller says so.

Expect the soft honey and malt of bud-rich Dian Hong and keep steeps short, though these are notes on the class rather than on this tea.

When buying, look at the leaf: even threads with plenty of gold and few broken bits.
history: Little is documented about when this name appeared or who used it first. It reads as a trade name within Dian Hong, not a tea with its own recorded history.
